title: Become all flame
hookLine: Abba Lot asks what more he can do, and Abba Joseph raises fingers like lamps: why not become all flame? (Sayings of the Desert Fathers)

cards: Say the good habits are built. The streak is going. You drink the water, take the walk, sit with the bell most days.
And one evening a small question slips in: is this it? Is there something more, and what is it? It's not a complaint.

It's a real question, and people have asked it for a very long time. In the Egyptian desert, a monk named Lot asked it out loud, to an older monk named Joseph. And Joseph answered without a single instruction.

teach.b: It's another story from the Sayings of the Desert Fathers, the same collection as yesterday's leaking basket. Abba Lot visits Abba Joseph and lays out his life honestly.
As far as I can, he says, I keep my little rule of prayer. I fast a little. I pray, and I keep quiet.
As far as I can, I keep my thoughts clean. What else should I do?
It's a humble list, and notice the phrase he keeps using: as far as I can. Joseph doesn't criticize any of it.

He stands up and stretches his hands toward heaven, and the story says his fingers became like ten lamps of fire. And he says to Lot: if you want, you can become all flame. That's the end of the saying.
The collection doesn't tell us what Lot did next. For the desert monks, the answer to what more should I do was not another item on the list.

teach.h: THE LIST IS THE FUEL, NOT THE POINT.
teach.b: The list is good; the list is the fuel. But the point was never to finish it. It was to be changed by what the list was for, all the way through.
In Christian teaching, especially in the Orthodox tradition, the saying is read as the life of God filling a person completely, a person transformed by God's light.

If you don't share that faith, the picture still speaks. There's a difference between doing a practice and being lit by it, between saying the words and meaning them with your whole self. Joseph didn't say pray more.

how: Monks and other Christians, especially in the Orthodox tradition, read Abba Joseph's saying as a call to be transformed by God completely; lighting a candle before prayer is a common practice in Orthodox and Catholic churches.

o: a monk who asked what else he should do
a desert elder who told Lot: become all flame
a Church father who wrote rules for monks

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: asks: what else should I do?

s: Abba Joseph scolds Lot for his small list
he doesn't criticize it at all. he stands and shows him the fire.
Joseph's fingers become like ten lamps of fire
then he says: if you want, you can become all flame.
the saying tells us what Lot did next
it stops with the fire. the collection doesn't say.

games.q: you're Abba Joseph. Lot has told you his humble rule of prayer and fasting, and asks what else he should do. what do you do?
o: give him a longer rule to keep
stand, lift your hands, and show him fire
tell him he's already done enough
games.why: he stands, stretches his hands toward heaven, his fingers become like ten lamps, and he says: if you want, you can become all flame.

practice: If you have a candle and a safe place for it, light it now; if not, a lamp will do, or picture one clearly. Watch the flame: it isn't one still thing, it moves, and it doesn't do fire partly.
When your mind starts a list, come back to the flame, and if you pray, hold Joseph's words in silence.

wordCard.voice: Abba Joseph. The desert elder who answered Lot's what else with ten fingers lit like lamps.

carryVoice: Your line: all flame. Not a longer list, but a whole self, lit. Until tomorrow.
